claims.claim: Bolt was born on 21 August 1986 (also behind the FAQ age answer: 40 as of 26 Oct 2026)
claims.note: Both sources give 21 August 1986. The arithmetic gives 40 on 26 Oct 2026. The Britannica snapshot says 'age 38', which is only a stale cache.

claims.claim: Born in Sherwood Content, a village in Trelawny parish, Jamaica (FAQ adds 'northern Jamaica')
claims.note: Olympics.com names Sherwood Content. Britannica gives Trelawny parish and calls it a 'town', not a village. 'Northern Jamaica' is in neither source, though it is geographically true. Minor.

claims.claim: As a boy he cared more about cricket and football than running; his high-school cricket coach pushed him into athletics
claims.note: Olympics.com says he excelled at football and cricket and that his cricket coach encouraged athletics. 'Cared more about... than running' is a mild inference.

claims.claim: In 2002, aged 15, he won the 200 m at the world junior championships
claims.note: Britannica says he was 15 and won gold in the 200 m.

claims.claim: Bolt's first 100 m world record came in May 2008
claims.note: Britannica says 9.72 in New York, four weeks after 3 May 2008. Olympics.com says 2007, which is wrong. The article is right to follow Britannica, but the person.json source list contains this disagreement.

claims.claim: At Beijing 2008 he lowered the 100 m record to 9.69
claims.note: World Athletics refers to the 9.69 set at the Beijing Olympics.

claims.claim: Jamaica's 4x100 m relay team, with Bolt, also won in world-record time in 2008
claims.note: Britannica gives a relay world record of 37.10.

claims.claim: Official count is eight Olympic golds, not nine
claims.note: Olympics.com lists 8G. It does not give the reason, which comes from ITV, and Britannica confirms the relay medal was stripped.

claims.claim: On 16 August 2009 in Berlin's Olympic Stadium he ran 9.58, taking 0.11 off his own record; Tyson Gay was second in 9.71, a national record
claims.note: All confirmed. 9.71 vs 9.58 is 0.13, so 'more than a tenth behind' is correct.

claims.claim: 200 m final four days later: 19.19, 0.11 faster than his Beijing time, 0.62 s margin; clock first showed 19.20 before correction
claims.note: Yahoo gives 20 Aug 2009, 19.19, 11 hundredths off his previous record, a 0.62 s margin, and an initial time of 19.20 revised to 19.19.

claims.claim: Both world records (9.58 and 19.19) still stood when the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo began
claims.note: The pre-championship record watch lists 9.58 and 19.19 (Bolt, 2009) as the world records.

claims.claim: At the 2011 Daegu Worlds Bolt was disqualified from the 100 m final for a false start; a single false start meant disqualification; Yohan Blake won in 9.92
claims.note: Disqualification, the immediate-DQ rule and Blake's 9.92 are all confirmed.

claims.claim: Won 100 m and 200 m at both London 2012 and Rio 2016; winner of the Olympic 100 m at three consecutive Games
claims.note: Both sources confirm.

claims.claim: Summary and knownFor: eight Olympic golds across three Games; retired after the 2017 World Championships
claims.note: Confirmed by the Olympics.com medal count and by Britannica on the three Games and the retirement.

claims.claim: Nationality: Jamaica (person.json facts)
claims.note: Olympics.com lists Jamaica.

claims.claim: Present-tense 'still holds' claims replaced by: World Athletics still listed both as world records in its record preview for Tokyo 2025
claims.note: Dated to the source; no present-tense claim remains in summary, opening or closing line.

claims.claim: January 2017: the IOC disqualified Jamaica's 2008 relay team; Nesta Carter's sample tested positive for methylhexaneamine; Bolt had to relinquish his medal
claims.note: ITV page opened in this re-check (25 Jan 2017): IOC, Carter, methylhexaneamine, 'has had to relinquish his medal'.

claims.claim: 12 August 2017, anchor leg of the 4x100 final, hamstring injury, fell; Britain won gold; retired with 14 World Championship medals
claims.note: Al Jazeera page opened: 12 Aug, anchor leg, hamstring, forward roll, Britain 37.47, '14 world career medals'.

claims.claim: Daegu 2011: false-start disqualification under the IAAF's immediate-disqualification rule; Blake won in 9.92
claims.note: Al Jazeera 2011 opened: immediate disqualification rule, Blake 9.92. 'Newly introduced/shortly before' timing removed.

claims.claim: Berlin 200 m on 20 August 2009 in 19.19 by 0.62; time first recorded as 19.20 then revised
claims.note: Yahoo opened: 20 Aug, 19.19, 0.62 margin, initial 19.20 revised. 'Scoreboard' wording removed.

claims.claim: Cricket coach encouraged him to take athletics seriously
claims.note: Olympics.com opened: 'his cricket coach encouraged him to take up athletics seriously'.

claims.claim: Added: Kingston 2002, youngest male world junior champion in any event; Athens 2004 hamstring, out in 200 m heats; Olympic 100 m record in London; Rio first to win both individual sprints at three straight Olympics; 1.96 m and the tall-sprinter belief
claims.note: Britannica opened in this re-check; all stated there.

claims.claim: Quote: 'I stopped worrying about the start. The end is what's important'
claims.note: Olympics.com opened: quote verbatim (translated in non-English versions, marked as such).

claims.claim: 'Two fastest sprint times in history' / 'same stadium' / 'north of Jamaica' wording removed
claims.note: Now 'two world records in the same city, four days apart', which WA and Yahoo support.

claims.claim: Beijing 200 m 19.30 world record beating Michael Johnson's 19.32 from Atlanta 1996
claims.note: Star Tribune opened (21 Aug 2008): matches.

valueNote: Clear timeline from Trelawny to London 2017, explains the eight-not-nine Olympic golds with the IOC ruling, the Daegu false start and the 19.20/19.19 correction, with dated record status.
summary: Re-check after fixes. 5 flagged claim(s) from the previous review were corrected or removed: Every flagged claim was fixed or removed and the sources the previous check could not open (ITV, Al Jazeera 2011/2017, Yahoo, Star Tribune, Olympics.com, Britannica) were opened in this re-check; the page was expanded with Britannica and Olympics.com facts.
